transcript.text:
If your dishwasher won't come on at all (no lights, no display), it usually means one of three things: it has no power, a safety lock is active, or the door isn't telling the machine it's shut. Please try these two quick checks:
1. Check the power source: Make sure the plug is firmly in the socket and that any wall switch (often a switched spur above the worktop) is turned on. If you have another small appliance, try it in that same socket to confirm electricity is reaching it.
2. Check for locks: Look at the control panel. Is there a key or padlock symbol lit up? This indicates the child or control lock is active, which stops the machine from starting. Let me know if the lights are completely dead or if you see that lock symbol.
Lights are completely dead, no lock symbol or anything. Other sockets and lights work fine. The switch above the worktop is on and its little light is lit.

The most likely cause is that an internal safety fuse has blown. This is a common failure point when the appliance receives power externally but won't turn on internally. 1. Unplug the dishwasher from the mains socket (or isolate it at the spur switch).
2. Remove the side panel (usually the left-hand one) to expose the internal electronics/control box.
3. Look for a small glass or ceramic tube fuse mounted on the circuit board.
4. Check if the thin wire inside is broken or if the glass is blackened. If the fuse is blown, it suggests an electrical fault inside (often a shorted component). If the fuse is intact, the issue is likely further down to the control board itself. Let me know what you see.
It's an integrated one so I can't pull it out to get at the side panel. Is there anything else I can check from the front? Not sure how to check the fuse in the spur either, and I've no spare.

Since the spur switch is most likely on and you can't easily access the side panel of an integrated unit to check the internal fuse yourself, we are left with two possibilities: either that internal safety fuse has blown (which protects the electronics from a short circuit), or the control board itself has failed. Because replacing a PCB is expensive and complex, and a blown fuse often indicates a deeper electrical fault inside the machine, this is likely beyond what can be safely fixed without specialist tools and parts. I would recommend calling an engineer to diagnose whether it's just the fuse (and why it blew) or if the board needs replacing. If you are handy with basic DIY and have access to a multimeter, you could try removing the bottom kickplate (usually held by two screws) and looking up into the base of the machine. Some models have a small glass fuse visible on top of the control box near where the power cable enters. If you see a broken wire inside that tube, it suggests the fuse is blown. However, if you are not comfortable doing this, or if the fuse looks fine but the machine still won't turn on, an engineer visit is the correct next step.

candidates: No power at the socket (plug, switch, fuse, or trip) (high)
Control lock / child safety lock engaged (medium)
Door not fully latched or latch fault (medium)
